g.passage: I had asked Younghee three times to write down the fish stew he made each winter, and three times he had laughed and pointed at the gulls over the ferry terminal, as though the birds kept his accounts. On the morning he meant to sail for his sister's island, I brought a notebook and a pencil to the waiting hall. He took neither. Instead he pressed a paper twist of dried anchovies into my palm, then a knob of ginger, then a pinch of something gray that smelled of smoke. __He named nothing, only closed my fingers over each in turn, the way a man coils rope he expects another to handle.__ When the horn sounded, he walked to the gangway without looking back. I stood a long while in the Busan wind, the notebook still blank under my arm, and found I no longer wished to fill it.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that Younghee has forgotten the ingredients and is hiding his confusion from the narrator.
It suggests that Younghee resents the narrator's repeated requests and wishes to end the visit.
It indicates that Younghee is handing down the recipe through touch rather than through writing.
It reveals that the narrator has finally persuaded Younghee to record the recipe in lasting form.
g.explanation: Younghee는 레시피를 적어 달라는 요청을 세 번 웃어넘겼고, 공책과 연필도 받지 않은 채 재료를 하나씩 화자의 손에 쥐여 준다. 밑줄 문장은 그가 이름을 말하지 않고 손가락을 감싸 주는 동작을, 다른 사람이 다룰 밧줄을 감는 선원의 습관에 빗대어 전수의 의미를 드러낸다. 마지막에 화자가 공책을 채우고 싶지 않게 된 것도 레시피가 이미 몸으로 전해졌음을 뒷받침하므로 C가 정답이다. A의 망각이나 B의 원망은 지문 근거가 없고, D는 공책이 끝까지 비어 있다는 점과 모순된다.

g.passage: Defne had ruled on harder matters than a broken dryer, but she watched Leopoldina kneel before the machine as if a verdict waited inside it. The girl had come from the courthouse on her lunch hour, still wearing her lanyard, with a screwdriver borrowed from the guard. 'The belt is worn,' Leopoldina said. 'I can tighten it. It will turn again for a month, perhaps two.' Defne said nothing about the rust spreading along the drum's seam, which she had noticed the first week the Istanbul laundromat opened. __She handed over her own coins for the test cycle and sat down to wait, folding her hands in her lap as she once had at the bench.__ The drum shuddered, caught, and began to spin. Leopoldina grinned up at her. Defne nodded slowly, the way she used to nod at lawyers whose arguments were well made and would not, in the end, prevail.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that Defne doubts Leopoldina's skill and plans to supervise every single step of the repair.
It suggests that Defne regrets leaving the courthouse and misses the authority of her old role.
It reveals that Defne expects the repair to last and wishes to reward the clerk's hard effort.
It conveys that Defne lets the clerk's attempt proceed respectfully despite knowing its limits.

g.passage: Four stones mark the safe path across the dry riverbed below our town in Oaxaca, and Nicolas taught me to count them aloud before I was old enough to ask why. Every crossing, my stepfather named them: the flat one, the split one, the one shaped like a shoe, the last. The summer my scholarship letter came, he walked me to the bus on the far bank. I, Katarzyna, the girl who had never left the valley, talked the whole way about tuition, about the cost of the ticket north, about how he would manage the stall alone. He answered none of it. __At the third stone he stopped, tapped it twice with his boot, and waited until I said its name.__ On the far bank he set down my suitcase and told me the river would be running by the time I came home, and that I should not try to cross it by memory.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows Nicolas answering the narrator's worries through a familiar ritual instead of discussion.
It suggests that Nicolas is unsure of the old path and needs the narrator to guide him safely across.
It indicates that Nicolas disapproves of the scholarship and is trying to delay her departure.
It reveals that the narrator has forgotten the stones and must be taught the path once again.
g.explanation: 화자는 등록금과 차비, 가게 운영 걱정을 쏟아내지만 Nicolas는 어느 말에도 대답하지 않는다. 대신 밑줄 문장에서 그는 어릴 때부터 함께 해 온 돌 이름 부르기 의식을 반복하게 하며, 말이 아닌 익숙한 행동으로 화자를 안심시키고 떠나보낸다. 마지막에 돌아올 때는 기억에 의존해 건너지 말라는 당부도 이 의식이 작별의 의미를 지님을 뒷받침하므로 A가 정답이다. B와 D는 길을 모른다는 근거가 없고, C는 그가 직접 버스까지 배웅한 사실과 맞지 않는다.

g.passage: Flour dusted my stepmother's wrists before the sun was up, and by five she had already shaped forty loaves for an oven she could no longer afford to repair. I was sixteen and had told her, more than once, that the bakery in our Tbilisi lane was finished: the new supermarket sold bread cheaper, and Stanislav, who had fired the oven for my father, was nearly eighty. She never argued. She only set out cups of tea each morning, one for herself and one for Stanislav, and a third, untouched, at my place on the bench. __One morning I sat down and drank it, and she slid the scoring blade across the table toward me without a word.__ I cut the loaves badly. Stanislav laughed until he coughed. Dmitri, my friend from school, asked that afternoon why my hands smelled of yeast, and I told him I was only helping until the place closed. I said that for eleven more years.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows the narrator finally convincing the stepmother that the bakery must be closed.
It marks the narrator's first acceptance of a role the stepmother had quietly kept open.
It suggests the stepmother is testing whether the narrator could replace Stanislav at the oven.
It reveals that the narrator joined the work only to prove the bakery could not survive.
g.explanation: 계모는 화자의 폐업 주장에 반박하지 않고 매일 아침 화자의 자리에 손대지 않은 차 한 잔을 놓아 둔다. 밑줄 문장에서 화자가 그 차를 마시자 계모가 말없이 칼을 건네는데, 이는 계모가 비워 둔 자리를 화자가 처음으로 받아들인 순간이다. 마지막에 '문 닫을 때까지만 돕는다'는 말을 11년 동안 했다는 대목이 그 수락의 지속을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A와 D는 화자가 결국 남았다는 결말과 어긋나고, C는 오븐 담당 교체를 시사하는 근거가 없다.

g.passage: When the band paused between songs, Tommaso came in through the kitchen door of the wedding hall as if he had stepped out for ice twenty minutes earlier instead of nine years. Aaliyah, the bride, did not know him; she saw only that her new mother-in-law set down her fork and did not pick it up again. He wore a pressed suit a size too large and carried a gift wrapped in newspaper. No one asked where he had been, and he offered nothing, only kissed his mother's cheek and took the empty chair by the cake table that someone, it seemed, had been keeping. Gossip along the Delta levees had long since called him a scoundrel. Yet the cake was cut beneath his hand, and the old woman ate two pieces, and the bride, watching, decided that some absences are settled in ways a guest list cannot show.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Tommaso?
options: The narrator is openly contemptuous of his failure to explain his long absence.
The narrator is amused chiefly by the awkwardness his arrival causes among the guests.
The narrator is indifferent to his history and attends only to the bride's feelings.
The narrator withholds judgment, implying his return holds meaning gossip overlooks.
g.explanation: 서술자는 Tommaso의 9년 공백을 설명하지 않으며, 그가 늦게 들어온 장면도 비난 없이 담담하게 그린다. 누군가 비워 둔 의자, 어머니가 케이크를 두 조각 먹는 모습 같은 행동 단서는 그의 귀환이 가족에게 의미가 있음을 보여 준다. 소문이 그를 악당이라 불렀다는 언급 뒤에 'Yet'으로 반전시키는 구조가 서술자의 유보적 태도를 드러내므로 D가 정답이다. A는 소문의 시각을 서술자의 시각으로 오독한 것이고, B와 C는 지문의 진지한 관찰과 맞지 않는다.

g.passage: Who tells a dying man that the salt works he built will be sold by spring? I asked Armand this on my third week, while we raked the evaporation pans outside Beirut and the crust cracked white under our boots. He did not answer. He told me instead to rake slower, so the crystals would not cloud. That evening we carried a tin of the first harvest to Giada's bed, and Armand described the pans to him in detail: how high the brine stood, how the wind had come off the sea. Every word was true. He left out only the letter from the buyers, folded in his breast pocket. Driving back, I said that wasn't lying, exactly. Armand turned the radio up. I have spent years since retelling that drive, and I always slow down at the part where he raked so carefully for a man who would never see the sale.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Armand?
options: Respectful of his care for Giada, though uneasy about what he chose to leave unsaid
Openly critical of what the narrator regards as Armand's deliberate deception of Giada
Dismissive of Armand's silence, which the narrator reads as indifference to his friend
Wholly approving of Armand's decision and certain that it was the only honest choice
g.explanation: 화자는 '모든 말이 사실이었다'고 강조하면서도 Armand가 매각 편지만은 빼놓았다는 점을 굳이 덧붙인다. 돌아오는 길에 '정확히 거짓말은 아니었다'고 말하는 대목에는 판단을 망설이는 불편함이 드러난다. 그러면서도 수년이 지나도록 그가 정성껏 갈퀴질하던 장면에서 늘 이야기를 늦춘다는 마지막 진술은 깊은 존중을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 비판의 강도가 과하고, C는 Armand의 세심한 행동과 모순되며, D는 화자의 머뭇거림을 무시한다.

seed.relationship: a teenage cook and her stern aunt
seed.conflict: about an ending that nobody wants to admit
seed.topicSeed: a metro platform in Manchester; a teenage cook and her stern aunt about an ending that nobody wants to admit

g.passage:
Hot oil still in my hair, I stand on the platform at Piccadilly
beside Chiara, who has said nothing since the till was counted.
Forty years she ran that kitchen like a ship,
barked at me for every bruised onion, every slack knife.
Tonight she wrapped the knives in a tea towel
and gave them to me, handle first,
the way she taught me, the way you pass something sharp.
Nobody said closing. The sign says Back Soon.
A Manchester tram comes in hissing. She checks her ticket twice.
I want to tell her the onions were never bruised,
that I learned the knife from her wrists, not her shouting.
Instead I hold the towel against my chest
and let her board first, the way she likes.
g.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Chiara?
options: Resentful of the years of harsh criticism Chiara directed at the speaker
Tender and protective, sensing the care beneath Chiara's strictness
Relieved that Chiara's demanding kitchen has finally been shut down
Puzzled by Chiara's silence and wary of provoking her bad temper
g.explanation: 화자는 Chiara가 양파와 칼 때문에 늘 호통쳤다고 회상하지만, 칼을 손잡이부터 건네받는 장면에서 그녀의 가르침을 그대로 따른다. '호통이 아니라 그녀의 손목에서 칼을 배웠다'는 행은 엄격함 뒤의 애정을 화자가 알아보고 있음을 보여 준다. 수건을 가슴에 품고 그녀가 좋아하는 대로 먼저 타게 하는 마지막 행동은 보호하려는 마음을 드러내므로 B가 정답이다. A는 과거 호통만 보고 오독한 것이고, C와 D는 '아무도 폐업이라 말하지 않는' 슬픈 분위기와 맞지 않는다.

g.passage: I was twelve when Mohan came home from the border and took over our grandfather's clock shop in Kochi, and I assumed he did it because no one else would. He was clumsy at first; his hands, which had cleaned rifles for six years, shook over the hairsprings. Still, every evening he cleared a space on the bench and set a loupe in front of me. I complained. Tourists bought quartz watches from the stalls; nobody, I told him, would pay to fix a pendulum. He agreed, and kept handing me the tweezers. I learned to hear the beat of an escapement before I learned to like him again. Now, when customers ask Sunja who taught her, I say my brother, and I let them assume he was a master. He was not. He was a man who practiced late at night so he could stay one lesson ahead of me.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mohan?
options: Resentful, since she believes he pushed an outdated trade onto her unwillingly
Admiring chiefly of the expert skill he showed as a master clockmaker
Affectionate and grateful, valuing his persistence more than his ability
Sympathetic toward him, though convinced that his effort was largely wasted
g.explanation: 화자는 Mohan의 손이 떨릴 만큼 서툴렀다고 솔직하게 말하면서도, 그가 매일 저녁 자리를 마련하고 핀셋을 건넸다는 행동을 반복해 보여 준다. 손님들이 그를 장인으로 여기게 두면서도 '그는 장인이 아니었다'고 덧붙이는 대목은 실력이 아닌 노력에 대한 애정을 드러낸다. 밤마다 한 수업 앞서 연습했다는 묘사가 이를 완성하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 초반의 불평만 본 오독이고, B는 서툴렀다는 진술과 모순되며, D는 화자가 결국 기술을 익혔다는 점과 맞지 않는다.

g.passage: Callum stepped off my father's boat in the summer of 1912 with a botanist's case and a cough, and asked within the hour why our tea bushes grew only on the western slope above the Galway shore. I was fourteen and found the question rude. Every child on the estate knew the east field was poor ground; my father, Lachlan, said so at supper each night, the way other men said grace. Callum walked the east rows anyway, crumbled the soil between his fingers, and said the trouble was the drainage ditch my grandfather had dug, not the earth. My father thanked him and refilled his cup. The ditch stayed. Callum left on the September ferry, and I rowed him across myself, cross that he had been right and that we would go on as if he had not. I still keep the soil sample he left on our windowsill, labeled in his small hand.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Callum?
options: Scornful of the arrogance he showed in questioning the family's knowledge
Fond of him chiefly because he flattered her father during the visit
Indifferent to his findings, which she regarded as unimportant to the estate
Grudgingly appreciative of the clarity that his outsider's view provided
g.explanation: 화자는 처음에 Callum의 질문을 무례하다고 느꼈지만, 그가 옳았다는 사실에 화가 났다고 고백한다. 그 분노는 Callum보다 아무 일 없다는 듯 살아갈 가족을 향한 것이어서, 그의 지적을 인정하고 있음을 보여 준다. 그가 남긴 흙 표본을 지금도 간직한다는 마지막 행동이 마지못한 존중을 드러내므로 D가 정답이다. A는 첫인상만 본 오독이고, B는 아첨의 근거가 없으며, C는 표본을 간직하는 행동과 모순된다.

g.passage: Taipei's hills were not supposed to hold vineyards, Mingyu told me, which was why he had planted one. We were strangers waiting out a washed-out road on his porch, my rented scooter tipped in the mud, rows of purple grapes dripping behind us. When I said my name was Xinyi, he repeated it twice, as if testing its weight. I asked how he had started. He said a teacher, forty years ago, had read his essay about his father's tea farm aloud and remarked, not unkindly, that it was a good essay about the wrong crop. He laughed telling it. Then he handed me shears and showed me how to cut a bunch without bruising its neighbors. By the time the road crew arrived, my hands were sticky and I had filled two baskets. I never learned what the teacher meant, and I doubt Mingyu had ever settled it.
g.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
options: To depict a traveler's frustration at being stranded far from her intended destination
To portray how an offhand comment became a lasting, unresolved motive in a man's life
To explain the farming methods needed to grow grapes in a poorly suited climate
To suggest that Mingyu bitterly resents the teacher who once dismissed his writing
g.explanation: Mingyu는 포도밭이 있을 수 없는 언덕이라서 오히려 포도밭을 심었다고 말하며, 그 계기로 40년 전 선생님의 한마디를 웃으며 꺼낸다. 화자가 그 말의 뜻을 끝내 알지 못하고 Mingyu도 풀지 못했을 것이라 짐작하는 대목은 그 말이 여전히 열린 질문임을 보여 준다. 따라서 지나가는 말 한마디가 평생의 일을 이끈 미해결 동기가 되었음을 그리는 것이 목적이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 화자가 오히려 수확을 도운 점과 맞지 않고, C는 세부를 과장했으며, D는 그가 웃으며 이야기한 점과 모순된다.

seed.relationship: a shopkeeper and a persistent customer

seed.topicSeed: a hospital waiting room in Hamburg; a shopkeeper and a persistent customer when old loyalties collide with new ones

g.passage: Burnt coffee and disinfectant: that is how I remember the waiting room in Hamburg where Annika found me. For eleven years she had bought her bread and her lottery tickets at my shop, and for eleven years she had argued with me about the price of everything. When my husband was admitted, I closed early for the first time since we opened. Annika arrived an hour later with a thermos and a bag of cheap rolls from the new chain bakery across the street, the very shop I had cursed to her face that month. 'Sadia,' she said, as if we stood at my counter. She did not apologize for the rolls. She only tore one in half and held it out. I ate it. They were not good. I have since stopped cursing the chain bakery, though I still refuse to stock its rolls, and Annika still argues with me over the price of mine.
g.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
options: To criticize the chain bakery for driving small neighborhood shops out of business
To describe the narrator's anxiety while she waits alone for news of her husband's condition
To show that a customer's care for the narrator mattered more than their daily disputes
To explain why the narrator finally decided to stock bread from the new bakery
g.explanation: Annika는 11년 동안 가격을 두고 화자와 다퉈 왔고, 화자가 욕하던 체인 빵집의 롤빵을 사 들고 병원에 나타난다. 사과 없이 롤빵을 반으로 찢어 내미는 행동은 사소한 충성의 엇갈림보다 화자를 향한 마음이 더 크다는 것을 보여 준다. 이후에도 두 사람의 다툼이 계속된다는 결말은 그 유대가 일상의 마찰과 공존함을 드러내므로 C가 정답이다. A는 화자가 욕을 멈췄다는 점과 맞지 않고, B는 배경 세부에 불과하며, D는 여전히 롤빵을 들이지 않는다는 진술과 모순된다.

seed.topicSeed: a printing press room in Vienna; a boy and the old man who sells him fish about borrowed money and borrowed time

g.passage: I was nine when Matthias, who sold herring from a cart outside the Vienna press where my father worked, began letting me pay him on Fridays instead of on the spot. He wrote nothing down. In the printing room, where I swept between the machines, every sheet was counted, every order logged in a ledger thick as a brick, and I assumed the whole adult world kept accounts that way. Matthias kept his in his head, or perhaps nowhere. When my father was laid off that winter, I owed him for six weeks of fish. I brought the coins in a twist of newsprint, and he took only half, saying the rest could wait until Linus was taller. He died before I was. I have worked among presses for forty years now, and the blank margin of a page still brings him back to me.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator regrets failing to repay a debt he owed to a local fish seller.
The narrator describes how his father's sudden job loss pushed the whole family into poverty.
The narrator explains how he came to choose a lifelong career in printing.
The narrator recalls a generosity that stood apart from the strict accounting around him.
g.explanation: 지문은 모든 종이와 주문을 장부에 기록하는 인쇄소와 아무것도 적지 않는 Matthias의 외상 방식을 대비시킨다. 아버지가 실직한 뒤 Matthias가 빚의 절반만 받고 나머지는 '키가 크면' 갚으라고 한 행동은 계산을 넘어선 너그러움을 보여 준다. 수십 년이 지나도 페이지의 빈 여백이 그를 떠올리게 한다는 결말이 그 대비를 다시 불러오므로 D가 정답이다. A는 후회라는 감정이 지문에 직접 드러나지 않고, B와 C는 배경 세부를 요지로 오독한 것이다.

seed.topicSeed: a lakeside dock in Naples; two estranged sisters over an unfinished project

g.passage: 'You kept the plans,' Salma said, not quite a question. Her sister, kneeling on the dock beside the half-built hull, did not look up. Their father, Mateo, had begun the boat the summer before he died, and the sisters had not spoken since the funeral, when they quarreled over whether to sell it. Now the frame lay on blocks by the lake outside Naples, its ribs gray with weather. Salma had come only to sign the papers. Instead she found herself holding a plank steady while her sister drove the nails, and then, without being asked, measuring the next one. Her hands remembered the spacing Mateo had taught them both. When the buyer's car pulled up at noon, Salma walked out to meet it and, after a short conversation, waved it away. She came back, picked up the measuring tape, and said nothing about the papers.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Salma most likely send the buyer away?
options: She believes the buyer has offered too little money for the unfinished boat.
Working on the boat has renewed her bond with her sister and their father.
She wants to punish her sister for having kept their father's plans secretly.
She realizes the boat is too damaged by weather to be worth selling now.
g.explanation: Salma는 서류에 서명하러 왔지만, 요청받지 않았는데도 언니를 도와 판자를 잡고 다음 판자를 잰다. 그녀의 손이 아버지 Mateo가 두 사람에게 가르친 간격을 기억한다는 대목은 작업이 아버지와 자매를 다시 이어 주고 있음을 보여 준다. 구매자를 돌려보낸 뒤 말없이 줄자를 다시 드는 행동이 이 동기를 뒷받침하므로 B가 정답이다. A의 가격 문제와 D의 손상 판단은 지문에 근거가 없고, C는 화해로 향하는 흐름과 반대된다.

seed.topicSeed: a courtyard with a dry fountain in Auckland; a sister and her younger brother's tutor about who gets credit for shared work

g.passage: I found Mele in the courtyard on the morning of the science fair, sitting on the rim of the dry fountain in our Auckland lodging house with my brother Nalani's volcano model on her knees. She had tutored him all winter; I had watched from the kitchen window as she held his wrists steady over the plaster and let him believe the idea for the vents was his. In fact it was hers. I had heard her suggest it. I told her so now, and said the judges ought to know. She only turned the little flag bearing his name so that it faced the gate. At the fair Nalani talked for ten minutes without stopping, his hands moving the way hers had. Mele stood at the back of the hall, and when he won, she was already walking home.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Mele most likely decline to claim credit for the vents?
options: She worries the judges would disqualify a project that a tutor had designed.
She is embarrassed that the vent design was less original than she claimed.
She values Nalani's confidence in the work more than recognition for herself.
She resents the narrator for exposing her role and wants to avoid an argument.
g.explanation: Mele는 겨울 내내 Nalani의 손목을 잡아 주며 분화구 아이디어가 그의 것이라고 믿게 두었고, 화자가 심사위원에게 알려야 한다고 하자 이름 깃발을 문 쪽으로 돌려 놓는다. 박람회에서 Nalani가 막힘없이 설명하는 모습은 그 자신감이 Mele가 의도한 결과임을 보여 준다. 그가 우승할 때 이미 집으로 걸어가고 있었다는 행동은 인정받는 것에 관심이 없음을 드러내므로 C가 정답이다. A와 B는 지문 근거가 없고, D는 Mele가 화자에게 화를 낸 흔적이 없다는 점과 맞지 않는다.

seed.conflict: over a decision made without asking
seed.topicSeed: a mountain bus stop in Chiang Mai; two night-shift coworkers over a decision made without asking

g.passage: Malek had already bought both tickets by the time I reached the bus stop above Chiang Mai, and I was angry before I had caught my breath. We had worked the same night shift at the guesthouse for two years, and we had always split everything, from noodles to taxi fares to the blame when a booking went wrong. The plan had been to decide together whether to take the early bus home for the holiday or wait another week. He had decided. When I asked why, he shrugged and said the early bus had better seats. I sulked for half the ride. Then, near the second switchback, I remembered telling him, weeks before and only once, that my mother's surgery was set for the fourteenth. The early bus arrived on the twelfth. Darnell, I told myself, you are not a person who notices things.
g.question: Based on the text, why did Malek most likely buy the tickets without consulting the narrator?
options: He preferred the better seats on the early bus and assumed the narrator would agree.
He had grown tired of the narrator's indecision about their holiday travel plans.
He wanted to avoid splitting the cost of the tickets as the two usually did.
He recalled the narrator's family situation and wanted the narrator home in time.
g.explanation: Malek은 이유를 묻자 좋은 좌석 때문이라고 둘러대지만, 이는 표면적인 핑계로 제시된다. 화자는 몇 주 전 단 한 번 어머니 수술 날짜가 14일이라고 말했던 것을 떠올리고, 이른 버스가 12일에 도착한다는 사실과 연결한다. 마지막에 화자가 스스로 눈치가 없다고 자책하는 대목은 Malek이 그 말을 기억하고 배려했음을 보여 주므로 D가 정답이다. A는 Malek의 핑계를 그대로 믿은 오독이고, B와 C는 지문에 근거가 없다.

seed.relationship: a mother and a daughter planning a wedding
seed.conflict: while learning to let go of a habit
seed.topicSeed: a kite-maker's yard in Bergen; a mother and a daughter planning a wedding while learning to let go of a habit

g.passage: Beneath the drying lines of the kite-maker's yard in Bergen, where Gunnar's paper birds hung waiting for wind, the mother and her daughter sat with the wedding list between them. The mother had a habit of tying knots in anything left near her hands: string, ribbon, the fringe of a shawl. Today it was the twine meant for the kite tails, and she had knotted half a spool before the daughter laid a hand over hers. Neither spoke of it. They spoke instead of Anselmo's cousins, who would need rooms, and of the fish, which must be fresh. At dusk Gunnar let a red kite loose from the hill, and it rose cleanly, its tail free of knots. The mother watched it a long while. Then she untied the last knot she had made and wound the twine back onto the spool, slowly, as though measuring something she meant to give away.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Tender and quietly wistful
Tense and openly anxious
Playful and lightly comic
Bitter and faintly resentful
g.explanation: 어머니의 매듭 묶는 습관과 이를 말없이 막는 딸의 손길은 갈등보다 조용한 배려를 보여 준다. 두 사람은 습관에 대해 말하지 않고 결혼식 준비 이야기만 나누며, 감정을 직접 드러내지 않는다. 매듭 없이 날아오르는 연과 마지막 매듭을 풀며 무언가를 내어 줄 준비를 하는 어머니의 모습은 놓아 보내는 아쉬움을 담고 있어 A가 정답이다. B의 불안, C의 희극성, D의 원망은 지문의 잔잔한 분위기와 맞지 않는다.

seed.relationship: an immigrant father and his English-speaking daughter
seed.conflict: over how to describe an accident honestly
seed.topicSeed: a flooded cellar in Karachi; an immigrant father and his English-speaking daughter over how to describe an accident honestly

g.passage: Karachi had flooded before, but never into our cellar, and my father, Minjun, stood on the third step in his good shoes watching the water carry his sacks of rice toward the drain. The insurance man, Ruwan, arrived at noon with a clipboard and asked me, because my English was better, to explain what had happened. My father spoke first in Korean, quickly: tell him the pipe burst, tell him the wall was old. I knew the truth was plainer. He had left the hatch open in the storm to air the shelves, as he always did. I looked at the clipboard, then at his shoes, ruined now. 'The hatch was open,' I said. Ruwan wrote it down. My father did not look at me for the rest of the afternoon, but that evening he set two bowls on the table instead of one, and filled mine first.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Somber and wholly despairing
Strained yet quietly tender
Indignant and accusatory
Detached and coolly clinical
g.explanation: 화자는 아버지가 시킨 거짓 대신 해치를 열어 둔 사실을 말하고, 아버지는 오후 내내 화자를 쳐다보지 않아 긴장이 흐른다. 그러나 저녁에 아버지가 그릇 두 개를 놓고 화자의 그릇부터 채우는 행동은 갈등 속에서도 애정이 이어지고 있음을 보여 준다. 이처럼 불편함과 조용한 다정함이 함께 흐르므로 B가 정답이다. A는 결말의 화해를 무시하고, C와 D는 화자의 섬세한 관찰과 맞지 않는다.

seed.conflict: over a secret discovered in a drawer
seed.topicSeed: a hillside terrace in Nairobi; twin brothers dividing a house over a secret discovered in a drawer

g.passage: 'Leave the drawer for last,' my brother Baraka said, and so of course it was the first thing I opened. We had come back to our mother's house on the terrace above Nairobi to divide it, room by room, the way twins divide everything: precisely, and with suspicion. Inside the drawer were letters, dozens, addressed to Wanjiru in a hand neither of us knew, tied with the green ribbon she wore to church. Baraka read one and set it face down. I read three. We did not say what they meant; we did not need to. The afternoon went on. We argued about the radio, the good chairs, who had broken the blue pitcher in 1994. Neither of us mentioned the letters again, and when we left, the drawer was the only thing in the house we had not divided. We had shut it together, each with one hand.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Openly grief-stricken and despairing
Carelessly light and broadly comic
Wry yet quietly solemn
Angry and sharply accusatory
g.explanation: '마지막에 열라'는 말에 오히려 서랍부터 열었다는 도입과 쌍둥이가 '정확하게, 의심하며' 나눈다는 표현에는 가벼운 아이러니가 담겨 있다. 그러나 낯선 필체의 편지를 발견한 뒤 두 사람은 의미를 말하지 않고, 사소한 물건만 두고 다투며 비밀을 피한다. 서랍을 함께 한 손씩 닫는 마지막 행동은 비밀을 함께 지키기로 한 엄숙함을 드러내므로 C가 정답이다. A는 감정 표출이 지문에 없고, B는 진지한 분위기를 무시하며, D의 분노는 근거가 없다.

seed.conflict: over a plan that depends on a lie
seed.topicSeed: a snowed-in cabin in Maui; cousins reunited at a funeral over a plan that depends on a lie

g.passage: Two days of snow on the mountain above Maui, one cabin, one lie: that was the arithmetic Folasade laid out for me the night after our grandmother's funeral. If we told the family the road had closed earlier than it had, we would not have to attend the reading of the will, and no one would see us fail to cry. 'You don't have to agree, Anahera,' she said, already typing the message. We had not seen each other in eight years, not since a summer when I told an adult the truth about something she had done, and she had gone home early. She looked up at me now, waiting. I took the phone, read her message, and corrected one detail so that it would be believed. Then I handed it back, and she sent it, and she made us both tea without asking how I took mine. She remembered.
g.question: Which choice best describes the relationship between the narrator and Folasade?
options: They remain hostile, and the narrator joins the plan only to avoid another argument.
Folasade dominates the narrator, who follows her lead without any hesitation.
They are close friends who have stayed in constant contact since childhood.
Despite a past rift, they are tentatively rebuilding trust through a shared act.
g.explanation: 두 사람은 8년 전 화자가 Folasade의 잘못을 어른에게 말한 뒤로 만나지 않았다는 과거의 균열이 제시된다. Folasade가 '동의하지 않아도 된다'며 화자의 반응을 기다리고, 화자가 직접 메시지의 세부를 고쳐 거짓말에 동참하는 행동은 서로를 다시 믿기 시작했음을 보여 준다. 화자의 차 취향을 기억한다는 결말도 끊어졌던 유대가 조심스럽게 회복되고 있음을 뒷받침하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 적대감의 근거가 없고, B는 화자가 주체적으로 고친 점과 맞지 않으며, C는 8년의 단절과 모순된다.
